title: AI data centres need large amounts of firm power that nuclear could supply
oneLiner: The newest argument for repeal: a customer that wants constant, emissions-free electricity and can pay for it.
body: Australia has more than 160 operating data centres and over 200 more proposed. The Coalition argues that lifting the ban would let private operators contract for nuclear power for these loads, without any public money, and that a legislated prohibition deters that investment before it is even assessed.
contextBackground: By 2026 the data-centre case had largely replaced coal replacement as the Coalition's stated reason for repeal. The energy minister called nuclear for data centres a 'pipe dream'; the shadow minister called refusing it a missed opportunity. The federal government is drafting national data-centre rules on power and water.
contextDisagreement: Whether data centres change the arithmetic: supporters say a willing private buyer removes the public-cost objection; opponents say the timeline objection is untouched, since data centres are being built now and nuclear is not.

evidenceItems.citation: The Nightly, 'Chris Bowen declares nuclear to power data centres a pipe dream', 25 August 2026

otherClaim.title: Australia should repeal its federal ban on nuclear power generation

claimItself.title: Australia should repeal its federal ban on nuclear power generation
claimItself.oneLiner: Whether the 1998 prohibition on nuclear power plants should be lifted. Repeal is a separate question from whether anyone would then build one.
claimItself.body: Two federal Acts prohibit the approval of a nuclear power plant anywhere in Australia. Repealing them would allow proposals to be assessed on their merits under the ordinary environmental, safety and planning regimes. Whether a plant would then be commercially viable, or built in time to matter, is argued below.

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: CSIRO's GenCost report finds firmed renewables the cheapest new-build electricity for Australia and large-scale nuclear the most expensive

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: Nuclear power cannot help with Australia's electricity prices or reliability in time to matter

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: The political fight over nuclear is distracting from solving price and emissions problems now

otherClaim.title: Modelling commissioned by the Australian Conservation Foundation found powering data centres with small modular reactors would cost billions of dollars a year more than solar with storage

claimItself.title: Modelling commissioned by the Australian Conservation Foundation found powering data centres with small modular reactors would cost billions of dollars a year more than solar with storage
claimItself.oneLiner: The 'Phantom Energy' report put the gap at between $6 billion and $11 billion a year.
claimItself.body: The report compared the cost of meeting projected data-centre demand with small modular reactors against large-scale solar and storage, and found the nuclear option several billion dollars a year dearer. It also noted that no commercial reactor has yet been built with the modular factory methods meant to bring costs down.
